searchText: > Has there been talk about using it to subsidize protocol development? I know it is contentious but it also feels like the way to have sustainable funding. I am of course not objective on this subject and have my own conflict of interests since my job falls into the category of jobs that could be funded by such a mechanism. <@!364458974906548225> I think it would be a terrible idea since it's much much easier to change the protocol to siphon away a bit more from the BASEFEE than before as it is to change it from nothing gets taken away to something nothing is a good schelling point "a bit" is not so you'll create a class of people who live from these fees and have an incentive to never make them go away but increase them more and more I don't like systems where incentives are terrible and we have to trust in the well being and nice attitude of people so glad to hear it goes into the direction of "All burned" An alternative could be to give core devs big stacks of ETH that're locked (for long time spans like e.g. 5-8 years). As holders of ETH they'd profit from the burning (as every ETH holder) > Has there been talk about using it to subsidize protocol development? I know it is contentious but it also feels like the way to have sustainable funding. I am of course not objective on this subject and have my own conflict of interests since my job falls into the category of jobs that could be funded by such a mechanism. Generally this gets shouted down on basis of us not having a credibly neutral protocol to determine whom to fund More generally, there is no known way for humans to build such a protocol. More more generally, EIP-1559 is already extremely complex, the biggest pushback seems to be that it's very hard to model such a wide-ranging change, and we're already likely going to make it more complex by adding the "escalator tip" so I'd strongly push back against anything that's not needed to ship a good V1. I think that the fact that the tip fails under certain circumstances is probably good enough to use the escalator tip instead, but beyond that, it seems like we get rapidly increasing complexity for rapidly diminishing returns. Also, I think it's probably good to aim to get this live on mainnet before a lot of the other 1.x changes (i.e. witnesses, binary trie) also have to go into an upgrade. "When a transaction is accepted into a block, the user pays not their current bid, but the price of the next-highest bid in queue" Why not the third highest bid or fourth? What if the highest 2 users overpaid? the escalator thing seems a bit convoluted to me <@456226577798135808> Where do you see that? https://blog.ethereum.org/2020/06/16/eth1x-1559/ Hmm, I don't remember that from the actual proposal... ok, weird Generally I agree with <@!552133098075193354> the escalator addition seems to add a lot of complexity. Not sure if worth the returns at all. I think there's a tendency of people wanting to "leave their mark" and this should be opposed. Don't let the protocol suffer out of desire of "being nice". but anyway.. I'm just a user. you'll do the right thing yeah that's fair If people want an escalator they can always just do it manually (eg. auto-rebroadcast with higher fee after 1 minute) That way also leaks less info to miners making it harder to exploit The UX on signing multiple transactions is *terrible*. Especially if you are using something like a hardware wallet. Also, due to propagation time you end up missing out some opportunity, and you have to increment in 12% increments (which is a pretty big jump each step). To be clear, I was arguing _for_ the escalator, but _against_ trying to do anything fancy with the burnt part of the fee for now. The "redistribute half the burnt fee to all miners" thing is tough, because on the one hand it's a complexity increase, on the other hand it's a security mitigation If we want to increase security we can just increase the block reward. <@!273808422753796097> is there a longer form write-up on that anywhere? If so, I'll link it to the next call agenda. That would be *way* less complex (just a single constant change) and it would give us more confidence on exactly how much security was being provided (not a function of congestion/usage). Also, increasing the block reward is easy to do "quickly" if we see issues on mainnet See the very bottom of https://notes.ethereum.org/Wjr1SnW-QaST7phX9C5wkg?view Thanks! <@!301186049323958275> it's not just about the raw total reward size, it's also about addressing the concern of miners benefitting by colluding to push the basefee down I still haven't seen, and would like to see, an actual attack described that is mechanistically sound. Has someone presented one yet? Each time I have heard people suggest this, they hand wave over important details. Most variations I have heard depend on 51% (or more) miner collusion, and if 51% of miners are colluding Ethereum has *much* bigger problems. The screenshotted section of that document basically says (with less sass), "this attack is not reasonable, but if you fail to realize that we can placate you by giving half of the burned fee back to miners". yeah that's fair btw, for those still concerned about occasional 2x block sizes, I just realized that there is yet another already existing source of up to 2x variability: gas refunds so long story short we've been handling block size variability just fine 😆
